sbh4.2:1.3: Three criteria of grossness at every level: lower planes are (1) more suffering, (2) less calm-abiding, (3) shorter-lived. *Alpāyuṣka-tarā* refers to cosmological life-spans — beings reborn in higher planes live longer. For meditative purposes, this connects felt brevity-of-states at lower planes (states keep dropping away) with felt persistence-of-states at higher planes.
sbh4.2:2.6: *Sac-chidra-sāntara* (with-cleft, with-interval) describes first-jhāna attention as *interrupted* — the *vitarka-vicāra* create momentary clefts where attention falters before re-grasping the object. *Niś-chidra-nirantara* (without-cleft, without-interval) is the second jhāna's seamlessly continuous attention. A precise phenomenological description of the 1st→2nd transition.
sbh4.2:3.6: *Prīti* (rapture) is unambiguously good at first and second jhāna, yet for the practitioner moving to third jhāna it must be recognized as *gross* — as a *citta-kṣobha-kara* (mind-disturbance-maker) that obstructs *nirantarā upekṣā*. The engine of the mundane path: what was the achievement of the prior level becomes the obstruction at the next.
sbh4.2:3.16: *Laghu laghv eva prajñayā pratividhyati* — 'lightly, lightly indeed, by wisdom he penetrates.' The mechanism of third jhāna: *prīti*-traces still arise but are met with quick wisdom rather than effortful suppression. The two stabilizing factors are *smṛti* (mindfulness) and *saṁprajanya* (clear-knowing).
sbh4.2:4.7: The third jhāna is the unique zone where calm-equanimity meets felt happiness. Below it, you get happiness without continuous equanimity; above it, you get equanimity without happiness. Why classical texts sometimes call the third jhāna the most pleasant attainment — it is structurally pleasant in a way no other attainment is.
sbh4.2:5.14: Asanga explicitly lists breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) among what is abandoned at the fourth jhāna. The breath itself ceases. A structural marker: if the breath has not become very subtle to the point of apparent cessation, fourth jhāna proper has not been entered.
sbh4.2:5.17: *Aniñjya* — without-movement, unperturbed. *Sarveñjitāyatana* — sphere of all-non-perturbation. The structural feature that makes fourth jhāna the launchpad for the formless attainments and the *abhijñā*. Fourth jhāna is a gateway state, not a destination.
sbh4.2:6.5: The transition from form-realm (4th jhāna) to formless (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) requires releasing three perception-categories simultaneously: form-perceptions (color), obstruction-perceptions (resistance/objects-as-blocks), and manifold-perceptions (the world of things). The release-mechanism: *vairāgya* for the first two, *amanasi-kāra* for the third.
sbh4.2:7.4: The most subtle of the formless transitions. The consciousness that has been resolving on space-as-infinite is *itself* infinite (because its object is infinite). The practitioner shifts the resolve to that consciousness. Formless attainments are recursive applications of the same cognitive operation, not increasingly abstract objects.
sbh4.2:8.3: The mechanism for moving to *ākiñcanyāyatana* is *via negativa*. The practitioner searches for an object beyond consciousness — and *fails to find* one. The failure to find is itself the resolution. 'Nothingness' is not a metaphysical claim about emptiness or void — it is the contemplative recognition that no further object is available.
sbh4.2:9.5: *Naiva-saṁjñā-nāsaṁjñāyatana* — perception is not *ceased* (that would be one of the non-conscious attainments below). It is reduced to *sūkṣmā saṁjñā nimittālambane pravartate* — a *subtle perception proceeding with sign-as-object*. There is barely-perception. Hence 'neither perception nor non-perception.' This is the structural endpoint of the *laukika* path (*bhavāgra*).
sbh4.2:10.2: Two attainments in which consciousness itself ceases. *Asaṁjñā-samāpatti* is reachable by ordinary persons (*pṛthag-jana*) — serious meditators without supramundane attainment. *Nirodha-samāpatti* requires *ākiñcanya-vairāgya* plus stream-entry-or-higher status — an attainment of the noble path, not just of meditative skill. The latter is the closest mundane experience of *nirvāṇa*.
sbh4.2:11.5: The five higher knowledges: range of supernormal powers, divine ear, knowing minds of others, recollection of past lives, divine eye (passing-and-arising of beings). A sixth, *āsrava-kṣaya* (destruction of outflows), is supramundane and not part of this *laukika*-path treatment. These are far outside the working territory of contemporary lay practice.
